strengths: Soundness: The Salience HiPPO time-warp derivation is clear and gives an exact interpretation of the scalar modulation as deformation of the history measure. The Volterra readout and minimum-norm associative-memory update are also presented in mathematically intelligible forms.

Originality/significance: The unifying idea—expressing adaptive weighting, nonlinear interactions, associative storage, multiple timescales, and forecast-dependent memory in explicit orthogonal-polynomial coordinates—is interesting and potentially useful for mechanistic analysis of sequence models.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized, and its figures connect internal mechanisms to behaviors rather than reporting only task metrics. The appendix provides useful derivations and many implementation details.

The authors appropriately acknowledge the interpretability/performance trade-off. The WikiText-2 results honestly show that all tested Zoo variants trail modern SSMs and that associative-memory HiPPO transfers particularly poorly; this candid limitation is a positive aspect of the evaluation.

The methods support streaming updates, and the paper discusses computational scaling, including the exponential cost of higher-order Volterra terms and the dense scale coupling of log-timescale Multiscale HiPPO.
Ethics: The work is low risk, makes no problematic human-subject or dataset claims, and does not present unresolved material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: The principal Multiscale HiPPO comparison is severely resource-unmatched. The proposed system uses n=16 and m=128, hence 2,048 state coefficients, while each vanilla baseline stores only 16 (and the entire four-timescale bank only 64). Nevertheless, the text calls the representation “parsimonious,” refers to a “fixed HiPPO coefficient budget,” and concludes that one system matches all single-scale baselines. This experiment does not establish superior compression or accuracy at equal memory or compute.

The associative-memory mathematics contains a concrete inconsistency. For the stated orthonormal Legendre features, K(x,x)=||phi(x)||^2 is not identically one and varies strongly with x (at an endpoint it is the sum of 2n+1). Figure 6 instead says diagonal entries equal one “by definition,” apparently displaying a normalized kernel, whereas the write rule uses the unnormalized kernel. The claim that orthonormality makes the evaluation-vector norm well-conditioned is also unsupported. Appendix C.3 says Figure 6 uses 16 coefficients, while its caption says 32.

The synthetic comparisons do not isolate the proposed mechanisms fairly. Models are parameter-matched but not matched for state size, activation memory, or update cost. Associative HiPPO is given an explicit write/read memory tailored to the task, while the one-layer Transformer lacks the depth and positional information needed for most-recent-pair retrieval. Appendix C.6 itself shows that a two-layer Transformer with positional embeddings reaches 98.9–99.7%, substantially weakening claims of an efficiency advantage. Mamba is not included on the selective task despite being the central conceptual comparator.

Empirical evidence is narrow and statistically weak. Table 1 reports single accuracies without seeds, uncertainty, or learning curves; only the Volterra experiment reports five runs. There are no capacity-matched ablations for polynomial order, memory dimension, salience parameterization, learned gates, or alternative explicit memories. Consequently, perfect performance on short, specially constructed sequences does not demonstrate robust long-range modeling.

Forecasting HiPPO is supported almost entirely by qualitative plots. The reduced rank d is not specified, no held-out quantitative forecasting errors are reported, and the split/evaluation protocol is unclear. The manuscript also calls its projection a “minimum-norm, whitened representation” without giving the corresponding projector formula. Since Q=T^T T depends on the state parameterization and estimator, the broader interpretation as an objective-induced geometry on histories needs more careful qualification.

The Volterra experiment uses only one separable rank-one quadratic benchmark whose correct model order is built into the proposed readout. The appendix also appears inconsistent about lag units: the true kernel is defined through tau_max=50, whereas the inferred kernel is evaluated on {0,...,49} times Delta t with Delta t=0.01 and a 0.375 timescale. This makes the visual kernel agreement difficult to audit.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the breadth of the submission. Both “Code available at” locations are blank. Important settings are missing, including random seeds, g_max and the precise time-varying discretization for Salience HiPPO, the number K of OU components and multiscale base timescale, the forecasting rank d and evaluation split, and language-model sequence length, batch size, epoch budget, and preprocessing. The language-model results likewise lack uncertainty.

Originality is uneven across the five-item “zoo”: polynomial Volterra readouts, a diagonalizable bank of timescales (which Appendix D.4 admits is not more expressive than independent systems), reduced-rank linear forecasting, and an external polynomial associative bank largely combine classical components. The paper does not compare sufficiently against related explicit-memory, fast-weight, kernel-memory, or adaptive-timescale approaches to establish what is genuinely new.

Presentation is polished at a high level but occasionally overstates the evidence—for example, “learns a parsimonious ... continuum of timescales” despite a finite 128-dimensional scale expansion and an unmatched state budget, and “baselines fail completely” despite the successful Transformer variants in the appendix. These issues, together with the kernel inconsistency, reduce confidence in the central conclusions.

strengths: Soundness: The Salience HiPPO time-reparameterization is cleanly derived, and the induced real-time history measure gives a useful interpretation of scalar adaptive updates.

Originality: Unifying Volterra readouts, adaptive time warping, polynomial associative memory, multiscale representations, and forecast-induced geometry under an explicit orthogonal-polynomial perspective is conceptually interesting.
Presentation: The manuscript is generally readable and well organized, with informative visualizations of salience, kernels, timescales, and predictive memories.
The appendices provide substantial mathematical and experimental detail, including task definitions, update equations, discretization choices, and several hyperparameters.

The authors appropriately acknowledge the interpretability-performance trade-off. In particular, they report that every evaluated HiPPO variant underperforms modern baselines on WikiText-2 and that associative-memory HiPPO performs very poorly there.
The work presents no evident material ethical risk, and it does not misuse its limitations discussion; the candid negative language-modeling results are valuable.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central empirical claims rest predominantly on small, mechanism-matched synthetic tasks. Several variants receive tasks almost directly encoding their inductive bias, so perfect accuracy does not establish a broadly useful or competitive sequence-modeling method.

The comparisons are not resource-fair. Multiscale HiPPO uses 16×128=2048 state variables while each reported single-scale system uses only 16, yet the paper calls the representation parsimonious and refers to a fixed coefficient budget. Appendix D.4 further concedes that the system is equivalent, after a rotation, to a bank of fixed-timescale HiPPO systems.

Likewise, the selective-copying system has 64×256 recurrent state entries and the associative model has a separate writable memory bank. Matching only trainable parameter counts against LSTMs, Transformers, and S4D does not control state capacity, memory, FLOPs, or architectural access to external writable storage.

The claimed efficient online updates are insufficiently substantiated. Input-dependent Salience HiPPO requires discretizing dynamics whose effective step changes with g(t), but the paper does not clearly specify the per-step numerical implementation or provide runtime, memory, stability, or scaling measurements. Volterra and multiscale variants also have explicitly high polynomial or dense-coupling costs.

Several mathematical or explanatory statements are questionable. For an unnormalized truncated orthonormal Legendre basis, the reproducing-kernel diagonal K(x,x)=sum_n phi_n(x)^2 is not identically one, contrary to Figure 6's caption, and orthonormality alone does not make ||phi(x)||² uniformly well-conditioned. The text also inconsistently describes Figure 6 as using 16 coefficients while the figure uses 32.

The forecasting component is largely qualitative. It gives no forecast-error comparison, uncertainty across trials, ablation, or comparison against standard linear prediction. Important choices such as the reduced rank are omitted, while claims about a minimum-norm whitened predictive memory are not fully derived in the appendix.

The synthetic tables report single accuracy values without error bars or repeated-run variability. The Volterra comparison uses different learning rates and reports cumulative training error rather than held-out predictive performance, making its convergence comparison inconclusive.

Significance: On the only real-data experiment, vanilla HiPPO+MLP and Salience HiPPO obtain test perplexities of 6.80 and 7.52 versus 5.54 for Mamba, while associative-memory HiPPO reaches 20.41. This substantially limits the demonstrated practical value of the proposed zoo.

Originality is uneven: polynomial Volterra expansions, scalar time warping, reproducing-kernel associative updates, banks of timescales, and reduced-rank linear forecasting are individually classical ideas. The manuscript does not sufficiently distinguish each construction from its closest prior form or establish that their aggregation yields a deeper new result.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance. Both advertised code locations are blank, and essential language-modeling details such as batch size, context or truncation length, epoch budget, complete architectures, initialization, seeds, and run counts are missing. The synthetic experiments also lack seeds and complete implementation details.

Presentation is polished at a high level but sometimes overstates evidence: phrases such as baselines 'fail completely,' continuous addressing being 'fundamentally mismatched' to language modeling, and the multiscale method being parsimonious are not justified by the limited configurations tested.

The impact statement is generic, though this is a minor issue for a low-risk methodological paper. More important limitations—resource-inequitable comparisons, numerical conditioning, and the narrow synthetic evaluation—are not discussed with sufficient specificity.

strengths: Soundness: The central constructive claim is largely supported: the paper gives explicit formulations for nonlinear Volterra readouts, salience-based time warping, polynomial associative memory, multiscale states, and forecast-induced history geometry, with derivations connecting each mechanism to an interpretable orthogonal-polynomial representation.

Originality: The unified “HiPPO Zoo” viewpoint is creative and intellectually useful. Although several ingredients individually resemble classical Volterra models, time reparameterization, kernel memory, scale banks, or reduced-rank regression, organizing them as explicit alternatives to mechanisms hidden inside modern SSMs provides new understanding.

Significance: The work offers a useful toolkit for scientific and streaming settings where inspecting what is retained in memory matters more than maximizing benchmark accuracy. The induced history measures, recovered Volterra kernel, learned memory addresses, and forecasting eigenfunctions make the mechanisms unusually tangible.

Presentation: The manuscript is clear, well organized, and visually effective. It distinguishes the five mechanisms cleanly, provides substantial mathematical and experimental detail in the appendices, and openly reports poor language-modeling performance rather than obscuring the interpretability–accuracy trade-off.

The task-aligned results are compelling demonstrations: Salience HiPPO reaches 100% on selective copying, Associative Memory HiPPO reaches 100% on associative recall, and the quadratic model recovers the qualitative structure of the known Volterra kernel.

Limitations and ethics are treated appropriately overall. The discussion acknowledges computational scaling, specialization, and inferior real-world predictive performance. The work appears low-risk, with no material ethical concern left unresolved.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is predominantly synthetic and tailored to each proposed mechanism. WikiText-2 is the only real-data experiment, and all proposed variants underperform the strongest baselines—sometimes drastically—so the practical significance beyond interpretability demonstrations remains uncertain.

The multiscale comparison is not capacity matched: the reported multiscale state has 16×128=2048 coefficients, whereas each single-scale baseline has only 16 coefficients and even the four-system bank has 64. Consequently, claims of parsimony or equal-or-better quality are not established under comparable state, memory, or compute budgets.

Some baseline conclusions are overstated. Associative recall depends on order and recency, yet the main transformer comparisons omit positional embeddings. Appendix C.6 shows that a two-layer transformer with positional embeddings reaches 99.7–98.9%, indicating that the headline failure of standard baselines is substantially an architectural mismatch rather than evidence that they cannot perform binding.

The associative-memory kernel description appears internally inconsistent. For a truncated orthonormal Legendre feature vector, K(x,x)=||phi(x)||² is generally position-dependent, not identically one, whereas Figure 6 states that diagonal entries equal one “by definition.” The update normalizes by this quantity, but the displayed kernel and claims about interference need a precise normalized-kernel definition.

Several evaluations lack robustness analysis. The main synthetic accuracy tables and WikiText results report single values without seeds, confidence intervals, or sensitivity to state size and hyperparameters; the Volterra comparison uses cumulative training error rather than a clear held-out generalization evaluation.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite extensive appendix details: the manuscript’s code-availability line contains no usable repository link, and the language-modeling experiment omits important information such as batch size, sequence/BPTT length, architectural specifications, training duration, and variance across runs.

The novelty of individual components varies considerably: polynomial Volterra readouts and scalar time warping are fairly direct constructions, the multiscale system is explicitly equivalent to a rotated bank of fixed-scale systems, and the forecasting geometry follows standard linear prediction. The contribution is therefore strongest as a synthesis and interpretability framework rather than as five independently novel methods.
